passage: I'm Pema, and in my second week at the start-up I noticed what nobody said out loud. The office lights were still on at ten every night, and people ate dinner at their desks. When the founder walked past, keyboards got louder. A missed target meant a group email naming the person. I asked Ganga, who sat beside me, whether it was always like this. She shrugged: “It's just how it is. You get used to it.” Around us, everybody nodded slightly, as if we were talking about the weather. I felt a strange dizziness, as if I'd walked into a room where everyone else could breathe underwater. I'm writing this down now because I suspect that in a month I won't see it at all.

qa.q: What happened when the founder walked past?
qa.a: The keyboards got louder when the founder walked past.

qa.q: What does Pema's “strange dizziness” suggest about how Pema feels in the office?
qa.a: Pema feels startled and out of step, because the long hours and fear of blame seem ordinary to everyone else but not to a newcomer.

qa.q: What could Pema do to keep the clear view Pema has now?
qa.a: Pema could keep writing down what stands out, talk to someone outside the company and check what feels normal with people from other workplaces.

qa.q: What might Ganga be feeling when she says, “You get used to it”?
qa.a: Ganga may have accepted the routine as the price of staying and may be trying to comfort Pema, without noticing how much she has adjusted.

grounding: A newcomer sees long hours, fear of the leadership and blame as ordinary because everyone else accepts them, and knows blending in would remove the clarity.

passage:
Onboarding coach's note, week 5.
Pema, who joined as an analyst, said in her first week, “Is it normal that nobody leaves before the director does?” I have watched her since. In week two she was still asking questions in team meetings. By week three she was eating lunch at her desk like the rest. Yesterday, when the director named a colleague in a group email for a missed number, everyone looked at their screens, and Pema did too. Afterwards she said, “I guess this is just how it works here.” I asked what she had noticed in week one. She paused a long time. I've suggested she write down what she sees, and we will talk next Friday.
Tushar

qa.q: What did Pema ask in the first week?
qa.a: Pema asked, “Is it normal that nobody leaves before the director does?”

qa.q: What might Pema be feeling when Pema says, “I guess this is just how it works here”?
qa.a: Pema may be giving in to the group's view and feeling some doubt, since the fresh clarity of week one has faded.

qa.q: What did Tushar suggest to help Pema keep seeing clearly?
qa.a: Tushar suggested that Pema write down what she sees and planned to talk again next Friday.

qa.q: What might it be like for the colleague named in the group email when everyone looked at their screens?
qa.a: That colleague may feel exposed and alone, since nobody spoke up or even looked up, and the silence makes the blame seem normal.

grounding: A newcomer sees fear of the leadership and blame as ordinary because everyone accepts them, and blending in slowly removes the clarity, seen by an onboarding coach.

passage:
Journal, Tuesday, 11:40 p.m.
Week two at the agency. Things I've noticed that nobody else seems to:
1. Nobody leaves before the boss, and the boss leaves at ten.
2. When the client presentation had a typo today, the boss asked, 'Whose slide?' before asking how to fix it. Three people looked at the floor.
3. Jaya, who's been here two years, eats lunch at her desk with one hand and types with the other. When I asked if she ever takes a full lunch, she laughed. 'Lunch is for people with small targets.'
4. Everyone says 'it's crazy but it's fun'. Nobody looks like they're having fun.
I'm writing this down because I can feel myself getting used to it. Yesterday I apologised for leaving at nine.
Reena

qa.q: At what time does the boss leave?
qa.a: At ten.

qa.q: Why is Reena writing these things down?
qa.a: Reena feels uneasy and a little alarmed, sensing the slide into accepting it after apologising for leaving at nine.

qa.q: What could help Reena keep seeing clearly?
qa.a: Keep the journal, protect a few fixed limits like a proper lunch, and talk with a trusted friend or mentor outside the agency.

qa.q: How might Jaya see her own habits?
qa.a: Jaya seems to see skipping lunch as normal, even a badge of big targets, after two years of blending in.

grounding: A newcomer sees long hours, fear and blame clearly while colleagues treat them as ordinary, and notices herself adapting.

passage: In the office of the sugar mill outside Kolhapur, Chetan, three weeks into his first job, noticed things the others no longer seemed to. The clerks arrived at eight and left only after the manager's jeep drove away, sometimes at nine at night. When a weighbridge slip went missing, the manager shouted in the corridor, and within minutes three people had blamed the tanker driver, who wasn't even there. Dhruv, who had joined only a year before Chetan, said, 'Don't take it to heart, that's just how he is.' He said it the way people talk about rain. At the tea stall, Chetan watched Dhruv flinch every time the jeep horn sounded. On the bus home, Chetan typed in his phone notes: 'Week three. Still shocked. Don't stop being shocked.'

qa.q: Who did three people blame for the missing weighbridge slip?
qa.a: The tanker driver, who wasn't even there.

qa.q: What does Chetan's phone note suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: Chetan feels shocked and uneasy, and worried about getting used to it like everyone else.

qa.q: What could Chetan do to keep his clear view without putting himself at risk?
qa.a: Keep noting what he sees, find one or two colleagues who also feel uneasy, and talk to a trusted mentor outside the mill.

qa.q: How might Dhruv be experiencing the culture after a year?
qa.a: Dhruv talks about it like the weather but flinches at the jeep horn, so he is likely still afraid underneath, just used to hiding it.

grounding: A newcomer sees long hours, fear and blame clearly while a colleague who has blended in treats them as normal.

passage: On his first Monday at the architecture studio in Hamburg, Siddiq noticed the lights. At nine at night every desk was still lit. Emil, who had been there two years, was eating cold pasta over his keyboard. When the director walked past, the room went quiet, and Emil straightened like a schoolboy. At Tuesday's meeting a late drawing was blamed on "someone in the team"; nobody asked who, and three people stared at their laptops. "It's just how it is here," Emil told him at the coffee machine, smiling in a tired way. That night Siddiq typed a note on his phone: "Week one: fear, late hours, blame. Why does no one blink?" Then he added a line: "Read this again in six months."

qa.q: What was Emil eating at nine at night?
qa.a: Emil was eating cold pasta over his keyboard.

qa.q: Why did Siddiq add "Read this again in six months" to the note?
qa.a: He was uneasy and worried that he too might stop noticing the fear and blame once they started to feel ordinary.

qa.q: What could Siddiq do to keep his fresh view without being swept along?
qa.a: He could keep writing down what he sees, talk with someone outside the studio, and set his own limits on late hours before they become habit.

qa.q: How does Emil seem to see the studio's culture?
qa.a: To Emil it has become normal; the tired smile and "just how it is" suggest he has stopped expecting anything different.

grounding: Siddiq, a newcomer, sees long hours, fear of the director and blame as strange while a longer-serving colleague treats them as ordinary.
